newsitem.title: USA: GM cuts lease price of EV1 to spark demand.
newsitem.headline: GM cuts lease price of EV1 to spark demand.

text.p: In an effort to spark demand for its ground-breaking EV1 electric vehicle, General Motors Corp. said Friday it will slash the monthly lease payment for the tear drop-shaped car by up to 25 percent.

GM said the EV1 and its charging unit will now lease for a combined $399 a month in southern California, down from $530 previously. In Arizona, where fewer government subsidies are offered on the car, the monthly payment will drop to $549 a month from $690.
GM also will make the new, three-year lease payments retroactive for the 176 people who have already leased EV1s.

Sales for the EV1 have fallen off to 25 in April from 70 in January, and the automaker believes the two-seat car's high cost and concerns about the lack of places to charge its batteries are to blame.
The car, equipped with lead-acid batteries, has a maximum range of about 70 miles between charges, but real world usage has often resulted in shorter ranges.
Although EV1 buyers include Hollywood actors and producers such as Ed Begley Jr. and "Baywatch" actress Alexandra Paul, only 176 of 800 "serious prospects" have taken the cars home, GM officials say.

"As we have talked with the remaining people, the top issues on their mind are customer cost and lack of a basic backbone of charging stations that they can count on for emergency charging as they travel," said Joseph Kennedy, vice president of sales, service and marketing for GM's Saturn unit, which is marketing the GM-brand EV1.

Kennedy said GM also has set aside $250,000 to subsidise installation of EV1 charging stations at restaurants, shopping malls and other public establishments. GM hopes the programme will increase the number of public charging stations in California and Arizona by 50 from the current number of 70, some of which are located at Saturn dealerships.

GM cut the lease prices by lowering the interest rate to 8 percent from 9.5 percent and by increasing the car's estimated resale value. In California, the changes bring the lease payments in line with those offered on many other mid-$30,000 luxury cars, such as the Lexus ES300 and the Cadillac Catera.
"We'll learn about the elasticity of demand with this move, just as we're learning everything else about this market," he said.

Kennedy said the new prices would not alter significantly GM's business plan for the EV1, which GM officials have said is not profitable. GM has built about 546 saleable EV1 cars since production began Nov. 14, of which 120 are being used as demonstration vehicles and 216 are in dealer inventories.

Production of the car, which makes extensive use of aluminum in its body construction, has not been reduced in response to the slow sales. GM officials have previously said that the EV1 plant in Lansing, Mich., is capable of building about 5,000 of the cars per year.

GM has said it hopes to introduce a nickel metal hydride battery, which could double the car's range, by late 1997 or early 1998. Both Honda Motor Co. Ltd. and Toyota Motor Corp. plan to use nickel metal hydride batteries in their electric vehicles, which will debut at about the same time.
